concept.name: Long strangle
concept.definition: A long strangle is the simultaneous purchase of an out-of-the-money put (lower strike) and an out-of-the-money call (higher strike) on the same underlying with the same expiration date. It is cheaper than a long straddle but requires a larger move in either direction to profit.
concept.intuition: You buy a cheaper ticket on a big move: the strikes are further apart so you pay less, but the stock has to travel further before either leg has value.
concept.mechanics: Cost = OTM call premium + OTM put premium; breakevens at expiration are call strike + total premium and put strike - total premium. Maximum loss is the combined premium if the underlying finishes between the strikes.
concept.formula: Payoff at expiration = max(S_T - K_c, 0) + max(K_p - S_T, 0) - (C + P), where K_c > K_p are the call and put strikes; breakevens = K_c + (C + P) and K_p - (C + P).
concept.failure_modes: Because both legs are OTM, the most likely outcome is a total loss of premium; moves that are large but arrive late still lose to time decay, and event-driven buyers pay inflated implied volatility that collapses after the event.
concept.misconceptions: Cheaper than a straddle does not mean better value: the lower premium reflects a lower probability-weighted payoff, not a bargain.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, buy the $105 call for $1.50 and the $95 put for $1.20 (total $2.70). XYZ must finish above $107.70 or below $92.30 to profit; anywhere between $95 and $105 loses the full $270.
